issues.legal_issue: A conclusive declaration that land is needed for a public purpose may be challenged only where the acquisition is a colourable exercise of power.
material_facts: The government declared the land necessary for limestone quarrying, and the statutory declaration stated that it was needed for a public purpose.
The limestone was used to produce cement, which was sold for profit, but the appellant did not establish that the government’s action was a colourable exercise of power.
The court left open whether producing cement as a commercial enterprise is itself a public purpose.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the public-purpose declaration failed because the appellant did not show a colourable exercise of power; the court did not decide whether commercial cement production is a public purpose.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 6(1) and 6(3) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government’s declaration that land is needed for a public purpose is conclusive, subject to challenge where the power was colourably exercised for a private purpose or no purpose. The court followed Smt. Somavanti v. The State of Punjab.

rule.if: public_purpose_acquisition and conclusive_public_purpose_declaration and not colorable_exercise_shown

predicates.public_purpose_acquisition: The government acquires land on the stated basis that it is needed for a public purpose.
predicates.conclusive_public_purpose_declaration: The government makes a statutory declaration that the land is needed for a public purpose.
predicates.colorable_exercise_shown: The challenger establishes that the government used its acquisition power for a private purpose or no purpose.

issues.definition: When a public-purpose acquisition has a conclusive declaration and no colourable exercise is established, the challenge to that declaration fails.

issues.legal_issue: Urgent possession under the special power for arable or waste land is unauthorized when the acquired land is neither arable nor waste.
material_facts: The acquired land was forest land covered with a large number of trees, including about one lakh trees.
The government directed the Collector to take possession before an award, and the Collector did so.
The court found that the land was not mainly used for ploughing and raising crops and was not desolate, barren land with little or no vegetation.
issues.conclusion: The government’s direction under section 17(1) and the Collector’s taking of possession under that subsection were ultra vires.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, permits urgent possession before an award only of waste or arable land. In that context, arable land means land mainly used for ploughing and raising crops, while waste land means land unfit for cultivation or habitation, desolate and barren, with little or no vegetation. The land’s character is a jurisdictional fact that a court may determine independently on certiorari. The court relied on R. v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White and Collins v. Minister of Health.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The government invokes an urgent land-acquisition procedure permitting possession before an award.
predicates.land_neither_arable_nor_waste: The land is neither mainly used for ploughing and raising crops nor barren, desolate land with little or no vegetation.

issues.definition: In an urgent land-acquisition proceeding, possession taken under the special power is unauthorized if the land is neither arable nor waste.

issues.legal_issue: The power to dispense with objections in an urgent acquisition cannot validly be exercised where the land does not meet the condition for urgent possession and the government has not properly applied its mind to that condition.
material_facts: The land was forest land with a large number of trees, rather than waste or arable land.
The government formed the opinion that the urgent-possession provision applied and directed that the objection procedure be dispensed with.
Because the land did not meet the statutory condition, the court concluded that the government had not honestly formed the relevant opinion or had failed to apply its mind to the relevant facts.
A subsequent declaration and further acquisition proceedings followed the decision to dispense with objections.
issues.conclusion: The direction dispensing with objections was ultra vires; the subsequent declaration and proceedings were invalid and without jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, connect the power to dispense with objections under section 5A to the applicability of the urgent-possession provisions. Although the government’s opinion is subjective, it may be challenged if the government did not apply its mind or acted mala fide; the court may infer failure to apply the mind where the land does not satisfy the statutory condition. The court relied on King Emperor v. Shibnath Banerjee, Jaichand Lal Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Estate and Trust Agencies Ltd. v. Singapore Improvement Trust, Ross Clunis v. Papadopoullos, and R. v. Australian Stevedoring Industry Board.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The government invokes an urgent land-acquisition procedure that can dispense with the ordinary objection process.
predicates.land_neither_arable_nor_waste: The land is neither mainly used for ploughing and raising crops nor barren, desolate land with little or no vegetation.
predicates.government_opined_urgent_power_applied: The government states that the urgent-possession procedure applies and dispenses with the ordinary objection process.

issues.definition: When an urgent acquisition concerns land that is neither arable nor waste, the government’s decision to dispense with objections and the subsequent acquisition proceedings are invalid if based on the stated application of the urgent power.

issues.legal_issue: A grant of land carries the underlying mineral and subsoil rights unless those rights were expressly or impliedly reserved.
material_facts: The historical grants conveyed the estate and everything appertaining to it, without reserving mineral rights to the government.
The estate was permanently settled, and the relevant settlement recognized proprietors as proprietors of the soil.
The grantee’s use of the land was not restricted to agriculture, and evidence of dealings and conduct supported the grantee’s ownership of mineral rights.
The limestone was quarried from the acquired land.
issues.conclusion: The appellant owned the minerals and subsoil rights, including the limestone, and was entitled to compensation for them.
issues.legal_principle: A transfer of the surface ordinarily conveys the minerals beneath it unless the grant contains an express or implied reservation. The court relied on the terms of the grants, the Benares Regulation 1 of 1795 and the permanent-settlement regulations for Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, and the principle discussed in Halsbury’s Laws of England and Mitchell v. Mosley. It also relied on Ranjit Singh v. Kali Dasi Debi, Hari Narayan Singh v. Sriram Chakravarti, Durga Prasad Singh v. Braja Nath Bose, and Sashi Bhushan Misra v. Jyoti Prasad Singh Deo concerning proprietary rights in the soil and minerals.

predicates.land_grant_conveys_estate_and_appurtenan: A grant conveys the land together with the estate or property appertaining to it.
predicates.no_mineral_reservation: The grant contains no express or implied reservation of the underlying mineral rights.

issues.definition: A grantee owns the underlying minerals and is entitled to compensation when the grant conveys the land and its appurtenances without reserving those minerals.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for restoration of land must be rejected when the claimant’s intermediary interest has validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
material_facts: The appellant sought restoration of possession of the acquired land.
In a separate judgment delivered the same day, the court held that the appellant’s intermediary interest in the estate had validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.
issues.conclusion: The claim for restoration of possession was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied its holding in the companion matter, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raja Anand Brahma Shah, that the intermediary interest had validly vested in the state under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1951, as amended.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_restoration_of_land: A claimant seeks restoration of possession of land in a court proceeding.
predicates.claimant_intermediary_interest_validly_v: The claimant’s intermediary interest in the land has validly vested in the state under land-reform legislation.

issues.definition: A claim for restoration is denied when the proceeding seeks return of land and the claimant’s intermediary interest has validly vested in the state.
